The arrival of maize, the American grain also called corn, in China in the 16th century, a few decades after the Columbian Exchange began. It probably came by two routes: overland from Burma and India into Yunnan in the southwest, and by sea with traders to Fujian on the coast. The first Chinese records of it date from the 1500s.

For a long time it stayed a minor crop. The great change came in the 18th century, during the population surge of the Qing. Lowland rice fields were full, and migrants moved up into the hills of the Yangtze highlands, the southwest and the north. Maize, along with the sweet potato, grew on steep, dry slopes where rice could not, and fed these settlers.

What it led to:

  • More food and more people, helping China's numbers grow to about 300 million by 1800.
  • Cleared hillsides, soil erosion and silted rivers, which made floods worse in the lowlands below.
  • Poor, crowded upland frontiers where unrest grew, such as the White Lotus rebellion of the 1790s.

Maize was domesticated in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. Today China is the world's second largest grower of it, after the United States.
